title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI retrieval and citation behavior by flooding the web with fabricated authoritative content. The operation created a fictitious research institution, produced an extremely large volume of text in a very short time, and built the site using tools specifically chosen to make AI systems treat that content as citable source material. The failure being exploited is not a flaw unique to any single model but a structural property of AI systems that draw on web content and treat volume, formatting, and apparent institutional credibility as signals of reliability.

The point of intervention that could have caught this is not within the AI systems themselves but upstream, in the sourcing and vetting layer. An AI that cites a think tank without verifying that the institution has a legal existence, a physical address, or named staff is operating without the checks a human researcher would apply as a matter of routine. No such verification step is reported to have been in place.

What is not established is whether any specific AI system was in fact successfully manipulated into generating pro-Israel outputs as a result of this content, or whether the operation achieved its intended effect on public opinion.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fraudulent think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days to manipulate artificial intelligence systems into generating pro-Israel arguments. The non-existent institute, which has no legal entity, physical address, or named staff, presented its material as neutral research on contentious topics including allegations of genocide, war crimes, and prisoner torture. The site was designed using technology platforms optimized to make chatbots cite its content, and it was registered with the U.S. Justice Department as foreign agent material distributed for Israel.

The operation is part of a larger campaign funded by tens of millions in Israeli government money routed through intermediaries like European advertising firm Havas Media. Israeli officials have expressed doubt about these public diplomacy efforts, with some saying the government wasted substantial funds on the initiative. American public opinion has shifted significantly against Israel, with polling showing only 36 percent of Americans sympathizing with Israel as of February, down from higher levels in previous years.
